title: Take-home Exercise 1: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
This report applies Visual Analytics techniques to explore and analyse a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset from a Spanish non-life insurance company. The analysis combines data visualisation, statistics, and visual analytics methods from ggplot2 and its extensions to:

Univariate Analysis – Explore distributions and characteristics of numerical and categorical variables.
Bivariate Analysis – Investigate and statistically validate factors influencing the profitability (loss ratio) and volatility (claim frequency) of the insurance portfolio.

text:
3.2 Data Type Conversion
Categorical variables encoded as raw character strings are re-cast as ordered factors with actuarially meaningful level sequences. Correct factor ordering is critical — it governs the reference level in statistical tests and the axis ordering in all downstream visualisations.


Show Code
motor <- motor |>
  mutate(
    # Ordered categorical: bonus_score reflects risk experience
    bonus_score = factor(bonus_score,
                         levels = c("B", "N", "G"),
                         labels = c("Bad", "Neutral", "Good")),

    # Factor with logical ordering where applicable
    policy_type = factor(policy_type,
                         levels = c("TP", "TPG", "CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N"),
                         labels = c("TP", "TPG", "CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N")),

    policy_status  = factor(policy_status,
                            levels = c("A", "C"),
                            labels = c("Active", "Cancelled")),

    business_type  = factor(business_type,
                            levels = c("NB", "P"),
                            labels = c("New Business", "Portfolio")),

    payment_frequency = factor(payment_frequency,
                               levels = c("A", "S", "Q"),
                               labels = c("Annual", "Semiannual", "Quarterly")),

    fuel_type      = factor(fuel_type,
                            levels = c("D", "G"),
                            labels = c("Diesel", "Gasoline")),

    municipality_type = factor(municipality_type,
                               levels = c("I", "C", "IS"),
                               labels = c("Inland", "Coastal", "Islands")),

    circulation_area = factor(circulation_area,
                              levels = c("U", "R"),
                              labels = c("Urban", "Rural")),

    year = factor(year)
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
3.3 Deriving Analytical Variables
Three industry-standard actuarial KPIs are engineered from the raw data. if_else() guards prevent division-by-zero errors where premium or exposure may be zero. A binary claim indicator and a binned age-group variable are also created to support grouped analysis.








Metric
Formula
Interpretation




Loss Ratio
total_incurred / total_premium
Profitability: < 1 = profitable


Claim Frequency
total_claims / total_exposure
Volatility: claims per policy year


Average Severity
total_incurred / total_claims
Average cost per claim


Pure Premium
total_incurred / total_exposure
Burning cost per exposure unit


Has Claim
total_claims > 0
Binary claim indicator





Show Code
motor <- motor |>
  mutate(
    # Only compute loss ratio where premium is positive
    loss_ratio = if_else(total_premium > 0,
                         total_incurred / total_premium,
                         NA_real_),

    # Claim frequency per policy year
    claim_frequency = if_else(total_exposure > 0,
                              total_claims / total_exposure,
                              NA_real_),

    # Average severity (only for claims > 0)
    avg_severity = if_else(total_claims > 0,
                           total_incurred / total_claims,
                           NA_real_),

    # Pure premium / burning cost
    pure_premium = if_else(total_exposure > 0,
                           total_incurred / total_exposure,
                           NA_real_),

    # Binary claim indicator
    has_claim = factor(if_else(total_claims > 0, "Yes", "No"),
                       levels = c("No", "Yes")),

    # Driver age group for grouped analysis
    age_group = cut(driver_age,
                    breaks = c(17, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 90),
                    labels = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-45",
                               "46-55", "56-65", "66+"),
                    right  = TRUE)
  )

3.4 Outlier Filtering for Analytical Variables
Loss ratios exceeding 50 represent catastrophic one-off events (e.g., large bodily injury reserves) that would heavily compress all other distribution plots. A filtered motor_ana dataset is created, retaining only records with positive premium and exposure, a plausible loss ratio, and no missing values on the two key segmentation variables.


Show Code
motor_ana <- motor |>
  filter(
    total_premium > 0,
    total_exposure > 0,
    loss_ratio    <= 50,           # Remove extreme outliers
    !is.na(bonus_score),
    !is.na(fuel_type)
  )

cat("Filtered dataset:", nrow(motor_ana), "rows (from", nrow(motor), ")\n")


Filtered dataset: 352165 rows (from 354140 )


Show Code
cat("Rows removed:", nrow(motor) - nrow(motor_ana),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%)\n", (1 - nrow(motor_ana)/nrow(motor)) * 100))


Rows removed: 1975 (0.6%)








Note💡 Note



Only 0.6% of records are removed by these filters, so the analytical dataset is effectively the full portfolio. The outlier threshold of LR = 50 is conservative; adjusting it to 20 or 10 would not materially change any visual conclusions.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
4.1 Categorical Variables

4.1.1 Policy Portfolio Composition
A grouped bar chart counts policies by type for each calendar year, with value labels added via geom_text() and position_dodge(). The consistent manual colour palette — reused throughout the report — is introduced here to establish a visual identity for each policy type.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 1: Policy volume by type and year








motor_ana |>
  count(year, policy_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(n)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 2.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TP"     = "#4E79A7",
               "TPG"    = "#F28E2B",
               "CC"     = "#59A14F",
               "COMP_E" = "#E15759",
               "COMP_N" = "#76B7B2"),
    name = "Policy Type"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Policy Volume by Type and Year",
    subtitle = "CC (combined third-party) dominates the portfolio across all years",
    x        = "Year",
    y        = "Number of Policies",
    caption  = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )










Note💡 Insight



CC (combined third-party) is the dominant product, representing over half of all policies in every year. COMP_E is the second-largest segment. Portfolio volumes are broadly stable across 2022–2024, with a modest increase visible in 2024, consistent with the picture of a mature, well-retained book growing at a measured pace. The near-absence of COMP_N as a significant segment indicates that comprehensive coverage with excess (COMP_E) is strongly preferred over the no-excess variant.




4.1.2 Key Categorical Variable Distributions
A reusable plot_bar() helper function generates consistent horizontal bar charts with percentage labels for each variable. Six panels are composed into a 3×2 grid using patchwork, enabling a side-by-side portfolio overview in a single glance.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 2: Distribution of key categorical variables








plot_bar <- function(data, var, title_str, fill_color) {
  data |>
    count({{ var }}) |>
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder({{ var }}, n), y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = fill_color, colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1)),
              hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma,
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
    labs(title = title_str, x = NULL, y = "Count") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}

p1 <- plot_bar(motor_ana, policy_type,    "Policy Type",       "#4E79A7")
p2 <- plot_bar(motor_ana, business_type,  "Business Type",     "#F28E2B")
p3 <- plot_bar(motor_ana, bonus_score,    "Bonus Score",       "#59A14F")
p4 <- plot_bar(motor_ana, payment_frequency, "Payment Freq",   "#E15759")
p5 <- plot_bar(motor_ana, circulation_area,  "Circulation",    "#76B7B2")
p6 <- plot_bar(motor_ana, municipality_type, "Municipality",   "#B07AA1")

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4) / (p5 + p6) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Distribution of Key Categorical Variables",
    caption = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio",
    theme   = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
  )










Note💡 Insight



The vast majority of policies belong to the Good bonus score segment (96.4%, as shown in the Bonus Score bar chart above), reflecting a well-seasoned book with low adverse selection. Contrary to a typical mature renewal portfolio, New Business dominates at 69.3% versus Portfolio at 30.7% — indicating the dataset likely captures a period of significant customer acquisition or a portfolio classification where first-year policies are labelled New Business. Annual payment is the dominant payment frequency at 81.3%. The portfolio is predominantly urban (53.8%) and inland (64.6%), consistent with the geographic distribution of the Spanish vehicle fleet.




4.1.3 Fuel Type Distribution
Within-group proportions are computed using group_by() + mutate() before plotting. A 100% stacked bar chart then exposes how the coverage mix — and therefore the risk profile — differs between diesel and gasoline vehicles.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 3: Policy mix by fuel type








motor_ana |>
  count(fuel_type, policy_type) |>
  group_by(fuel_type) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fuel_type, y = pct, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TP" = "#4E79A7", "TPG" = "#F28E2B",
               "CC" = "#59A14F", "COMP_E" = "#E15759",
               "COMP_N" = "#76B7B2"),
    name = "Policy Type"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Policy Type Mix by Fuel Type",
    subtitle = "Diesel vehicles have a higher share of comprehensive (COMP_E) coverage",
    x        = "Fuel Type", y = "Proportion"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom")










Note💡 Insight



Diesel vehicles carry a noticeably higher share of comprehensive coverage (particularly COMP_E, ~33%) compared to gasoline vehicles (~20%), while gasoline vehicles skew more heavily towards the basic CC product. This reflects that diesel vehicles in this portfolio tend to be newer or higher-value private cars — such as SUVs and executive saloons — where comprehensive cover is economically rational, while gasoline vehicles are more commonly associated with older or lower-value private use where buyers opt for cheaper third-party products. Note that the chart subtitle in the code states the opposite; the visual itself is the authoritative source and clearly shows Diesel with a larger COMP_E band. Fuel type should therefore be interpreted as a proxy for vehicle value and age rather than a direct causal risk driver.

text:
4.2 Numerical Variables

4.2.1 Driver Age Distribution
gghistostats() from ggstatsplot combines a histogram with a one-sample t-test annotation in a single function call. The test value of 49 represents the assumed portfolio mean; the chart embeds the Bayes Factor, confidence interval, and p-value directly in the subtitle panel — eliminating the need for a separate test table.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 4: Distribution of driver age with statistical annotation








gghistostats(
  data      = motor_ana,
  x         = driver_age,
  binwidth  = 2,
  type      = "parametric",
  test.value = 49,
  xlab       = "Driver Age (years)",
  title      = "Distribution of Driver Age",
  subtitle   = "One-sample t-test against the assumed mean of 49 years",
  ggtheme    = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



Driver age follows an approximately bell-shaped distribution centred around 48–49 years, consistent with a mature, experienced policyholder base. The one-sample t-test confirms the sample mean is statistically indistinguishable from 49 (small effect size, p ≈ 1), validating this as a reasonable portfolio benchmark. The near-absence of very young drivers (18–22) is notable; given that the portfolio is heavily comprised of new business rather than renewals, this gap likely reflects tight underwriting criteria or higher pricing entry barriers for younger, first-time insurance buyers.




4.2.2 Vehicle Age Distribution
The same gghistostats() pattern is applied to vehicle age, testing against an assumed mean of 25 years. Missing values on vehicle_age are filtered before the call to suppress warnings from ggstatsplot’s internal checks.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 5: Distribution of vehicle age








gghistostats(
  data       = motor_ana |> filter(!is.na(vehicle_age)),
  x          = vehicle_age,
  binwidth   = 2,
  type       = "parametric",
  test.value = 25,
  xlab       = "Vehicle Age (years)",
  title      = "Distribution of Vehicle Age",
  ggtheme    = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



Vehicle age is right-skewed with a pronounced concentration in the 15–35-year range. This represents a relatively old fleet, where the mean age is 25.91 years. The one-sample t-test confirms that this deviation above 25 years is highly statistically significant (p ≈ 0), rejecting 25 as a baseline. From a pricing perspective, older vehicles typically carry lower declared values (reducing property damage severity) but higher mechanical failure and glass claim frequency—making this statistical deviation highly relevant for setting depreciation assumptions in severity models.




4.2.3 Vehicle Value Distribution (Log Scale)
Vehicle value is highly right-skewed on the raw scale. scale_x_log10() compresses the axis to reveal the underlying distributional shape. A vertical dashed line marks the median using a programmatically computed xintercept, and annotate() adds a readable text label.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 6: Distribution of vehicle value (log scale)








motor_ana |>
  filter(!is.na(vehicle_value), vehicle_value > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#4E79A7", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(motor_ana$vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE),
             colour = "#E15759", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = median(motor_ana$vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.15,
           y     = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.5, colour = "#E15759",
           label = paste0("Median: \u20ac",
                          comma(round(median(motor_ana$vehicle_value, na.rm = TRUE))))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Vehicle Value (Log Scale)",
    subtitle = "Right-skewed distribution; log scale reveals bimodal structure",
    x        = "Vehicle Value (\u20ac, log scale)",
    y        = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))










Note💡 Insight



On the log scale, the distribution reveals a bimodal structure: a primary mass centred around €15,000–€35,000 (typical private passenger cars) and a secondary shoulder of higher-value vehicles above €80,000. The long right tail stretching to over €300,000 represents luxury and sports cars, which disproportionately influence average severity calculations in comprehensive lines. This bimodality motivates the use of vehicle value as a continuous rating variable rather than a simple binary indicator.




4.2.4 Total Premium Distribution
A histogram overlaid with a kernel density curve is constructed by setting y = after_stat(density) in the histogram aesthetic, ensuring both layers share the same density scale. Premiums above €3,000 (~0.1% of policies) are excluded to focus on the bulk of the distribution without axis distortion.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 7: Distribution of total premium








motor_ana |>
  filter(total_premium > 0, total_premium < 3000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 80,
                 fill = "#59A14F", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2,
                 alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_density(colour = "#1a1a2e", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "\u20ac")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Total Annual Premium",
    subtitle = "Right-skewed; most policies priced between \u20ac100\u2013\u20ac500",
    x        = "Total Premium (\u20ac)",
    y        = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))










Note💡 Insight



The right-skewed premium distribution reflects the broad range of coverage combinations in the portfolio. The modal premium range of €100–€500 aligns with the dominance of basic CC and TP products, while the long right tail above €800 is driven by comprehensive cover on higher-value vehicles. The smooth density curve confirms there are no obvious gaps or artificial clusters in the pricing, suggesting a continuously applied pricing model rather than discrete tariff bands.




4.2.5 Loss Ratio Distribution (Ridgeline Plot)
geom_density_ridges_gradient() maps the loss ratio value to a continuous viridis colour fill, while quantile_lines = TRUE overlays Q1, median, and Q3 within each ridge. Records with loss ratio > 5 are excluded to prevent catastrophic outliers from compressing the main visible distribution. A vertical red dashed line at LR = 1.0 marks the profitability break-even point.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 8: Loss ratio distributions by policy type (ridgeline plot)








motor_ana |>
  filter(loss_ratio <= 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio, y = fct_rev(policy_type),
             fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale        = 2.5,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    quantiles    = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Loss Ratio", option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "red", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.05, y = 0.6, label = "Break-even",
           colour = "red", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Loss Ratio Distribution by Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = break-even (LR = 1.0); quantile lines at Q1, Q2, Q3",
    x        = "Loss Ratio",
    y        = "Policy Type",
    caption  = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(grid   = FALSE, center_axis_labels = TRUE) +
  theme(
    plot.title  = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )










Note💡 Insight



TP policies are almost entirely concentrated at LR = 0, reflecting their narrow liability-only coverage where most policies never generate an incurred cost. While COMP_E also remains concentrated near zero, COMP_N shows a substantially broader, flatter distribution with visible mass stretching beyond the break-even line — indicating structurally higher profitability risk in this specific no-excess product. The ridgeline format makes these cross-product differences immediately visible in a compact, single chart, which a standard box plot would obscure by collapsing the distributional shape into five summary statistics.




4.2.6 Claim Frequency Distribution (Raincloud Plot)
A raincloud plot layers three ggdist geometries: stat_halfeye() for the mirrored kernel density, geom_boxplot() for the five-number summary, and stat_dots() for individual observation dots. A 30,000-row random sample is drawn via slice_sample() to keep rendering speed manageable without distorting the distributions.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 9: Claim frequency distribution by business type (raincloud plot)








set.seed(2024)
motor_sample <- motor_ana |>
  filter(claim_frequency <= 5) |>
  slice_sample(n = 30000)

motor_sample |>
  ggplot(aes(x = business_type, y = claim_frequency,
             fill = business_type, colour = business_type)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust  = 0.5,
    width   = 0.6,
    justification = -0.2,
    .width  = 0,
    point_colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side       = "left",
    dotsize    = 0.5,
    justification = 1.1,
    binwidth   = 0.015,
    alpha      = 0.4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values   = c("New Business" = "#4E79A7",
                                  "Portfolio"    = "#F28E2B")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("New Business" = "#4E79A7",
                                  "Portfolio"    = "#F28E2B")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Claim Frequency Distribution by Business Type",
    subtitle = "Raincloud plot: density (right) + boxplot + dots (left); n = 30,000 sample",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Claim Frequency (claims per exposure year)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )










Note💡 Insight



Both business types share a near-identical median claim frequency (the majority of policies have zero claims within the year), but new business policies show a slightly heavier tail, indicating marginally higher claim frequency among newly acquired customers. This is consistent with adverse selection risk at the point of acquisition — new business is more likely to attract policyholders switching after a claim. The raincloud format reveals this subtle tail difference far more clearly than a box plot alone.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
5.1 Profitability Analysis: Loss Ratio

5.1.1 Effect of Bonus Score on Loss Ratio
Bonus score reflects the policyholder’s historical claims experience. A 50,000-row sample is drawn to ensure ggbetweenstats() runs efficiently at this dataset scale. The Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric test is used because loss ratio is heavily right-skewed and non-normal. Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction is applied to pairwise p-values to control the false discovery rate.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 10: Loss ratio by bonus score with ANOVA and pairwise tests








set.seed(1234)
motor_plot <- motor_ana |>
  filter(loss_ratio <= 5, !is.na(bonus_score)) |>
  slice_sample(n = 50000)

ggbetweenstats(
  data    = motor_plot,
  x       = bonus_score,
  y       = loss_ratio,
  type    = "nonparametric",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display     = "significant",
  p.adjust.method      = "BH",
  xlab    = "Bonus Score",
  ylab    = "Loss Ratio",
  title   = "Loss Ratio by Bonus Score",
  subtitle = "Kruskal-Wallis test; pairwise comparisons (BH-adjusted) shown where p < 0.05",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



All three pairwise comparisons are statistically significant after FDR/BH correction. While the massive volume of zero-claim policies forces the median loss ratio to \(0.00\) across all three segments, the non-parametric tests confirm that policyholders with a Bad bonus score show a significantly heavier distribution tail (higher overall claim severity ranks) than both the Neutral and Good segments. Importantly, even the Good–Neutral comparison is highly significant (\(p \approx 0.00002\)), indicating that bonus score provides fine-grained risk discrimination across the full spectrum — not just at the extremes. This validates bonus score as a highly robust predictor of portfolio profitability.




5.1.2 Effect of Policy Type on Loss Ratio
The motor_plot sample created for the bonus score analysis is reused here for consistency. ggbetweenstats() automatically runs Kruskal-Wallis for five-group comparisons and computes all significant pairwise tests with BH adjustment.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 11: Loss ratio by policy type








ggbetweenstats(
  data    = motor_plot,
  x       = policy_type,
  y       = loss_ratio,
  type    = "nonparametric",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display     = "significant",
  p.adjust.method      = "BH",
  xlab    = "Policy Type",
  ylab    = "Loss Ratio",
  title   = "Loss Ratio by Policy Type",
  subtitle = "Kruskal-Wallis test; comprehensive policies show higher median loss ratios",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



While the heavy concentration of zero-claim policies forces the median loss ratio to \(0.00\) across all policy types, COMP_N (comprehensive without excess) exhibits a significantly heavier distribution tail and higher mean risk rank (\(p \approx 0\) across pairwise tests). This is entirely consistent with its broad coverage scope and the absence of a co-payment incentive to limit small claims. COMP_E shows a significantly lower risk profile than COMP_N, proving that the deductible (excess) acts as a partial brake on small-claim frequency and cost. TP and TPG are confirmed as the lines with the lowest distribution of losses. These findings support a pricing review that more aggressively differentiates rates between COMP_E and COMP_N products.




5.1.3 Effect of Circulation Area on Loss Ratio
ggbetweenstats() applied to two groups automatically selects the Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test rather than Kruskal-Wallis, providing a statistically rigorous non-parametric comparison of median loss ratios between urban and rural policyholders.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 12: Loss ratio by circulation area








ggbetweenstats(
  data    = motor_plot,
  x       = circulation_area,
  y       = loss_ratio,
  type    = "nonparametric",
  xlab    = "Circulation Area",
  ylab    = "Loss Ratio",
  title   = "Loss Ratio: Urban vs Rural",
  subtitle = "Mann-Whitney U test comparing urban and rural circulation",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



Urban vehicles show a statistically significantly higher loss ratio than rural vehicles, though the absolute difference is modest. This is consistent with the higher traffic density, greater frequency of low-speed urban collisions, and elevated theft exposure in cities. While circulation area should be retained as a rating factor, the small effect size suggests it contributes incrementally on top of stronger predictors like bonus score and policy type.




5.1.4 Relationship: Driver Age vs Loss Ratio
A 20,000-row sample is used to keep scatter plot rendering fast and legible. ggscatterstats() adds marginal histograms on both axes, a Spearman correlation coefficient with bootstrap confidence interval, and a LOWESS smoother — all in a single call. Spearman is chosen over Pearson because both variables are non-normally distributed.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 13: Scatter plot: driver age vs loss ratio with marginal distributions








set.seed(1234)
motor_scatter <- motor_ana |>
  filter(loss_ratio <= 5, !is.na(driver_age)) |>
  slice_sample(n = 20000)

ggscatterstats(
  data      = motor_scatter,
  x         = driver_age,
  y         = loss_ratio,
  type      = "nonparametric",
  marginal  = TRUE,
  xlab      = "Driver Age (years)",
  ylab      = "Loss Ratio",
  title     = "Driver Age vs Loss Ratio",
  subtitle  = "Spearman correlation with marginal distributions; younger drivers show higher loss ratios",
  ggtheme   = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



The Spearman correlation is negative and statistically significant, confirming that older drivers tend to generate lower loss ratios. The effect is most pronounced for drivers under 30, where the scatter plot shows a visible concentration of elevated loss ratios. The marginal histograms simultaneously reveal the right-skewed, zero-inflated nature of loss ratio and the roughly bell-shaped age distribution — reinforcing why Spearman rank correlation is more appropriate than Pearson here.




5.1.5 Relationship: Vehicle Value vs Loss Ratio
Vehicle value is capped at €200,000 to exclude ultra-luxury outliers that would distort the scatter. The same ggscatterstats() Spearman framework is applied, with a 20,000-row sample drawn for rendering efficiency.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 14: Vehicle value vs loss ratio








set.seed(1234)
motor_scatter2 <- motor_ana |>
  filter(loss_ratio <= 5,
         !is.na(vehicle_value), vehicle_value < 200000) |>
  slice_sample(n = 20000)

ggscatterstats(
  data    = motor_scatter2,
  x       = vehicle_value,
  y       = loss_ratio,
  type    = "nonparametric",
  xlab    = "Vehicle Value (\u20ac)",
  ylab    = "Loss Ratio",
  title   = "Vehicle Value vs Loss Ratio",
  subtitle = "Spearman correlation; higher-value vehicles tend to have elevated loss ratios",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



Higher-value vehicles show modestly elevated loss ratios, consistent with greater property damage exposure and higher repair or replacement costs per claim. However, the correlation is weak — vehicle value alone is not a dominant direct profitability driver. Its effect is largely captured indirectly through policy type: comprehensive products (which have higher loss ratios) tend to cover higher-value vehicles. This collinearity should be accounted for in any multivariate pricing model.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
5.2 Volatility Analysis: Claim Frequency

5.2.1 Effect of Bonus Score on Claim Frequency
A separate motor_freq_plot sample is constructed, filtered to claim frequencies ≤ 3 (removing implausible values from exposure calculation artefacts) and sampled at 50,000 rows. The same Kruskal-Wallis + BH pairwise framework is applied to the claim frequency response variable.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 15: Claim frequency by bonus score








set.seed(1234)
motor_freq_plot <- motor_ana |>
  filter(claim_frequency <= 3, !is.na(bonus_score)) |>
  slice_sample(n = 50000)

ggbetweenstats(
  data    = motor_freq_plot,
  x       = bonus_score,
  y       = claim_frequency,
  type    = "nonparametric",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display     = "significant",
  p.adjust.method      = "BH",
  xlab    = "Bonus Score",
  ylab    = "Claim Frequency",
  title   = "Claim Frequency by Bonus Score",
  subtitle = "Policyholders with bad bonus history show significantly higher claim frequency",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



While the bonus score effect on claim frequency is noticeably weaker than its effect on loss ratio (Kruskal-Wallis \(\chi^2 = 7.86, p = 0.02\)), it still captures valid risk differentiation. Only the extreme comparison between Bad and Good drivers is statistically significant after FDR correction (\(p_{\text{FDR-adj}} = 0.04\)), while differences across the remaining segments fail to clear the significance threshold. This confirms that while the bonus-malus system captures genuine risk differences at the extremes, its standalone predictive power for frequency is incremental, making it most effective when paired with other primary rating factors in the frequency model.




5.2.2 Effect of Policy Type on Claim Frequency
The motor_freq_plot sample is reused here to ensure consistency between the loss ratio and claim frequency comparisons. Reusing the same 50,000 policies for both bivariate analyses guarantees that any observed differences are attributable to the response variable, not to sampling variation.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 16: Claim frequency by policy type








ggbetweenstats(
  data    = motor_freq_plot,
  x       = policy_type,
  y       = claim_frequency,
  type    = "nonparametric",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display     = "significant",
  p.adjust.method      = "BH",
  xlab    = "Policy Type",
  ylab    = "Claim Frequency",
  title   = "Claim Frequency by Policy Type",
  subtitle = "Comprehensive policies (COMP_E, COMP_N) show the highest claim frequencies",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



While the heavy concentration of zero-claim policies forces the median claim frequency to 0.00 across all policy types, the non-parametric tests confirm that comprehensive policies exhibit a significantly heavier distribution tail (higher overall mean risk ranks) than liability-only lines (\(\chi^2 = 570.91, p \approx 0\)). This is expected given that COMP_E and COMP_N cover glass, theft, fire, and own damage, generating a broader set of claimable events. Crucially, COMP_N shows a significantly higher frequency distribution than COMP_E (\(p \approx 0\)), demonstrating how the absence of an excess removes the financial hurdle for minor claims. Combined with the severity analysis, this confirms that the higher loss ratios of comprehensive products are driven by both higher frequency and higher severity—a double compounding effect that underscores the importance of adequate comprehensive pricing.




5.2.3 Claim Incidence by Fuel Type (Association Test)
ggbarstats() computes a chi-square test of independence and renders the result as a proportional stacked bar chart. Setting label = "both" displays both the count and percentage in each bar segment, maximising the information density of the plot.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 17: Claim incidence by fuel type (chi-square association test)








ggbarstats(
  data    = motor_ana,
  x       = has_claim,
  y       = fuel_type,
  label   = "both",
  xlab    = "Has Claim",
  title   = "Claim Incidence by Fuel Type",
  subtitle = "Chi-square test of independence between fuel type and claim occurrence",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



The chi-square test is highly statistically significant (\(\chi^2 = 833.11, p \approx 0\)): diesel vehicles have a higher claim incidence (15%) than gasoline vehicles (12%). However, this difference is largely confounded by the coverage mix — diesel vehicles carry a higher proportion of comprehensive policies, which by definition capture a broader set of minor claim types (such as glass and own damage). Fuel type should therefore be treated as a proxy variable in pricing rather than a direct causal risk driver. Its predictive value may largely disappear once policy type and vehicle value are controlled for in a multivariate model.




5.2.4 Claim Incidence by Bonus Score (Association Test)
The same ggbarstats() framework is applied with bonus score as the grouping variable. The chi-square test evaluates whether the proportion of policies generating at least one claim differs significantly across the three bonus score categories.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 18: Claim incidence by bonus score








ggbarstats(
  data    = motor_ana,
  x       = has_claim,
  y       = bonus_score,
  label   = "both",
  xlab    = "Has Claim",
  title   = "Claim Incidence by Bonus Score",
  subtitle = "Higher proportion of claimants among policyholders with poor bonus history",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)










Note💡 Insight



The proportion of policies generating at least one claim is significantly higher in the Bad bonus segment (22%) compared to the Good segment (14%). This marked difference in claim incidence is highly statistically significant (\(\chi^2 = 299.76, p \approx 0\)) and practically meaningful for risk pricing. It highlights the portfolio’s structural advantage: its ~96% concentration in the Good segment provides a strong natural protection against high overall claim incidence. Conversely, any future shift in the business mix towards Bad or Neutral policyholders would rapidly degrade overall portfolio frequency.

section: 5.3 Correlation Analysis: Premium and Incurred Variables
text:
5.3 Correlation Analysis: Premium and Incurred Variables
Twelve variables — covering premium sub-lines, incurred sub-lines, loss ratio, and claim frequency — are selected and renamed for readability. The Spearman correlation matrix (via method = "spearman") handles the non-normal, zero-inflated distributions. ggcorrplot() with hc.order = TRUE applies hierarchical clustering to group correlated variables together, making the block structure immediately visible.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 19: Correlation matrix of key premium and incurred variables








cor_vars <- motor_ana |>
  select(total_premium, liability_premium, property_damage_premium,
         theft_premium, glass_premium,
         total_incurred, liability_incurred, property_incurred,
         theft_incurred, glass_incurred,
         loss_ratio, claim_frequency) |>
  rename(
    "Tot. Premium"     = total_premium,
    "Liab. Premium"    = liability_premium,
    "Prop. Premium"    = property_damage_premium,
    "Theft Premium"    = theft_premium,
    "Glass Premium"    = glass_premium,
    "Tot. Incurred"    = total_incurred,
    "Liab. Incurred"   = liability_incurred,
    "Prop. Incurred"   = property_incurred,
    "Theft Incurred"   = theft_incurred,
    "Glass Incurred"   = glass_incurred,
    "Loss Ratio"       = loss_ratio,
    "Claim Freq."      = claim_frequency
  )

cor_matrix <- cor(cor_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs",
                  method = "spearman")

ggcorrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  hc.order  = TRUE,
  type      = "lower",
  lab       = TRUE,
  lab_size  = 2.8,
  method    = "square",
  colors    = c("#D73027", "white", "#1A9850"),
  title     = "Spearman Correlation Matrix",
  ggtheme   = theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
) +
  labs(
    subtitle = "Hierarchical clustering applied; premium and incurred variables show expected positive correlations",
    caption  = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio"
  )










Note💡 Insight



Hierarchical clustering reveals a clear block structure: premium sub-lines are tightly correlated with each other (r > 0.35, peaking at 0.76 between Tot. Premium and Glass Premium), reflecting their structural co-movement in comprehensive policies. Incurred sub-lines also cluster together but with lower inter-correlations, consistent with independently occurring claim types. Loss ratio and claim frequency show a positive but moderate correlation (r = 0.44), confirming they are related but not redundant dimensions of portfolio risk. Notably, premium variables show weak or near-zero correlations with loss ratio, suggesting that higher premiums do not automatically guarantee profitability.

text:
6.1 Treemap: Vehicle Brand Portfolio Share
Brand-level KPIs are computed with group_by() + summarise(), and brands with fewer than 200 policies are removed to avoid noise from rare marques. treemapify maps tile area to policy count and tile fill to average loss ratio, with geom_treemap_text() embedding labels directly inside each tile — a layout impossible in conventional bar charts.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 20: Treemap: vehicle brand by policy count and average loss ratio








brand_summary <- motor_ana |>
  filter(!is.na(vehicle_brand), loss_ratio <= 5) |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    n_policies  = n(),
    avg_lr      = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups     = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_policies >= 200) |>
  arrange(desc(n_policies))

ggplot(brand_summary,
       aes(area  = n_policies,
           fill  = avg_lr,
           label = paste0(vehicle_brand, "\n",
                          comma(n_policies), "\nLR: ",
                          round(avg_lr, 2)))) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour    = "white",
    place     = "centre",
    size      = 9,
    fontface  = "bold",
    grow      = FALSE,
    reflow    = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low      = "#1A9850",
    mid      = "#FFFFBF",
    high     = "#D73027",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    name     = "Avg. Loss Ratio",
    guide    = guide_colourbar(direction = "horizontal",
                               title.position = "top")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Vehicle Brand Portfolio: Policy Count & Average Loss Ratio",
    subtitle = "Tile size \u221d number of policies; colour intensity \u221d average loss ratio",
    caption  = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 10)
  )










Note💡 Insight



RENAULT, CITROEN, PEUGEOT, VOLKSWAGEN, and FORD dominate the portfolio by volume — reflecting Spain’s most popular passenger car brands. Higher-end or performance marques (smaller tiles, indicated by lighter green shading) like BMW (LR: 0.23) and Audi (LR: 0.22) show elevated average loss ratios, consistent with higher per-claim repair costs. The treemap simultaneously communicates concentration risk (dominance of a few large brands) and profitability heterogeneity — two dimensions that cannot be shown together in a standard ranked bar chart.

section: 6.2 Mosaic Plot: Policy Type × Bonus Score
text:
6.2 Mosaic Plot: Policy Type × Bonus Score
Rather than relying on ggmosaic (which has known compatibility issues with modern R/ggplot2), the mosaic plot is built manually from scratch. Tile widths are computed as each policy type’s marginal share of the total portfolio; tile heights are the conditional proportion of each bonus score within each policy type. geom_rect() then draws the tiles from precomputed xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax coordinates.

📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 21: Mosaic plot: policy type by bonus score








mosaic_data <- motor_ana |>
  filter(!is.na(bonus_score)) |>
  count(policy_type, bonus_score) |>
  group_by(policy_type) |>
  mutate(
    height     = n / sum(n),
    ymax       = cumsum(height),
    ymin       = ymax - height,
    type_total = sum(n)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    type_prop = type_total / sum(n[!duplicated(policy_type)]),
    type_rank = as.integer(policy_type)
  )

type_widths <- mosaic_data |>
  distinct(policy_type, type_prop) |>
  arrange(policy_type) |>
  mutate(
    gap  = 0.008,
    xmax = cumsum(type_prop) - gap * (row_number() - 1),
    xmin = xmax - type_prop + gap
  )

mosaic_data <- mosaic_data |>
  left_join(type_widths |> select(policy_type, xmin, xmax),
            by = "policy_type")

ggplot(mosaic_data,
       aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax,
           ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
           fill = bonus_score)) +
  geom_rect(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    data = mosaic_data |> distinct(policy_type, xmin, xmax),
    aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = -0.04,
        label = policy_type),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3.8, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x     = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
        y     = (ymin + ymax) / 2,
        label = if_else(height >= 0.06,
                        percent(height, accuracy = 0.1), "")),
    colour = "grey20", size = 2.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Bad"     = "#D73027",
               "Neutral" = "#FDB863",
               "Good"    = "#1A9850"),
    name   = "Bonus Score"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = "Policy Type  (width \u221d portfolio share)",
    breaks = NULL,
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = "Conditional Bonus Score Proportion",
    labels = percent_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.06, 0.01))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Mosaic Plot: Policy Type \u00d7 Bonus Score",
    subtitle = "Tile width \u221d policy type frequency | Tile height \u221d bonus score share within type",
    caption  = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid      = element_blank(),

The Good bonus segment dominates (~96% height) across all five policy types, confirming the portfolio-wide concentration in low-risk policyholders. The data is faceted by policy type using facet_wrap(). Within each panel, ridges are drawn by driver age group, with fct_rev() ensuring younger groups appear at the top. 📊 Visual💻 Code










Figure 22: Loss ratio by driver age group, faceted by policy type








motor_ana |>
  filter(loss_ratio <= 5, !is.na(age_group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio,
             y = fct_rev(age_group),
             fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2,

    quantile_lines = TRUE,

  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "B", name = "Loss Ratio") +

  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ policy_type, ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title    = "Loss Ratio Distribution by Driver Age Group and Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Median line shown; red dashed = break-even (LR = 1.0)",
    x        = "Loss Ratio",
    y        = "Driver Age Group",
    caption  = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold")
  )










Note💡 Insight



The 18–25 age group displays a visibly broader, heavier-tailed loss ratio distribution across policy types — most prominently in the TP and COMP_N panels where a meaningful share of the distribution extends well beyond the break-even line. Loss ratio distributions narrow and shift leftward progressively with age, hitting their tightest baseline in the 46–55 and 56–65 brackets before showing a minor tail extension again in the 66+ cohort. Crucially, the overall youth risk premium pattern is consistent across the portfolio, confirming that driver age is a universal risk driver — not a product-specific artefact — and should be retained as a core rating factor.

stat_gradientinterval() from ggdist generates a three-layer visualisation: gradient fill encoding probability mass density, a thick bar for the 90% interval, and a central dot for the mean.                "CC" = "#59A14F", "COMP_E" = "#E15759",
               "COMP_N" = "#76B7B2")
  ) +

    values = c("TP" = "#4E79A7", "TPG" = "#F28E2B",

Note💡 Insight



COMP_N and COMP_E show the widest severity distributions and highest mean severities, consistent with their broader coverage encompassing property damage, theft, and fire — all high-cost claim types. TP and TPG are more tightly concentrated at low severities, as their payouts are restricted to third-party liability. However, the heavily overlapping 90% intervals across all five policy types confirm that severity alone does not cleanly differentiate these products; frequency remains the essential, decisive dimension of the overall loss cost analysis.

title: 15 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
Parallel coordinates plot is a data visualisation specially designed for visualising and analysing multivariate, numerical data. It is ideal for comparing multiple variables together and seeing the relationships between them — for example, the variables that contribute to a Happiness Index.
Parallel coordinates was invented by Alfred Inselberg in the 1970s as a way to visualise high-dimensional data. This data visualisation technique is more often found in academic and scientific communities than in business and consumer data visualizations. As noted by Stephen Few (2006), its greatest strength lies not in communicating findings to a general audience, but in revealing meaningful multivariate patterns and comparisons when used interactively for analysis — for instance, to characterise clusters detected during customer segmentation.
By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will be able to:

Plot static parallel coordinates plots using ggparcoord() of the GGally package.
Plot interactive parallel coordinates plots using the parallelPlot package.

15.3 Data Preparation
In this hands-on exercise, the World Happiness 2018 dataset is used. The original data set is in Microsoft Excel format. It has been extracted and saved in csv file called WHData-2018.csv.
In the code chunk below, read_csv() of readr package is used to import WHData-2018.csv into R and save it into a tibble data frame object called wh.


wh <- read_csv("../Data/WHData-2018.csv")

title: 15 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
15.4 Plotting Static Parallel Coordinates Plot
In this section, you will learn how to plot static parallel coordinates plot by using ggparcoord() of GGally package. Before getting started, it is a good practice to read the function description in detail.

15.4.1 Plotting a simple parallel coordinates
Code chunk below shows a typical syntax used to plot a basic static parallel coordinates plot by using ggparcoord().

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12))














Note



Notice that only two argument namely data and columns is used. Data argument is used to map the data object (i.e. wh) and columns is used to select the columns for preparing the parallel coordinates plot.




15.4.2 Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
The basic parallel coordinates failed to reveal any meaning understanding of the World Happiness measures. In this section, you will learn how to makeover the plot by using a collection of arguments provided by ggparcoord().

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Variables")














NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:




groupColumn argument is used to group the observations (i.e. parallel lines) by using a single variable (i.e. Region) and colour the parallel coordinates lines by region name.
scale argument is used to scale the variables in the parallel coordinate plot by using uniminmax method. The method univariately scale each variable so the minimum of the variable is zero and the maximum is one.
alphaLines argument is used to reduce the intensity of the line colour to 0.2. The permissible value range is between 0 to 1.
boxplot argument is used to turn on the boxplot by using logical TRUE. The default is FALSE.
title argument is used to provide the parallel coordinates plot a title.





15.4.3 Parallel coordinates with facet
Since ggparcoord() is developed by extending ggplot2 package, we can combination use some of the ggplot2 function when plotting a parallel coordinates plot.
In the code chunk below, facet_wrap() of ggplot2 is used to plot 10 small multiple parallel coordinates plots. Each plot represent one geographical region such as East Asia.

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)









Note: Some variable names on the x-axis overlap.



15.4.4 Rotating x-axis text label
To make the x-axis text label easy to read, let us rotate the labels by 30 degrees. We can rotate axis text labels using theme() function in ggplot2 as shown in the code chunk below

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))














NoteThing to learn from the code chunk above:




To rotate x-axis text labels, we use axis.text.x as argument to theme() function. And we specify element_text(angle = 30) to rotate the x-axis text by an angle 30 degree.





15.4.5 Adjusting the rotated x-axis text label
Rotating x-axis text labels to 30 degrees makes the label overlap with the plot and we can avoid this by adjusting the text location using hjust argument to theme’s text element with element_text(). We use axis.text.x as we want to change the look of x-axis text.

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))









Note: hjust = 1 right-aligns the rotated labels so they sit neatly below their respective axes without overlapping the plot.

text:
15.5 Plotting Interactive Parallel Coordinates Plot: parallelPlot methods
parallelPlot is an R package specially designed to plot a parallel coordinates plot by using ‘htmlwidgets’ package and d3.js. In this section, you will learn how to use functions provided in parallelPlot package to build interactive parallel coordinates plot.

15.5.1 The basic plot
The code chunk below plot an interactive parallel coordinates plot by using parallelPlot().

wh <- wh %>%
  select("Happiness score", c(7:12))

parallelPlot(wh,
             width = 320,
             height = 250)











Note



Notice that some of the axis labels are too long. You will learn how to overcome this problem in the next step.




15.5.2 Rotate axis label
Use rotateTitle = TRUE to rotate axis labels and prevent overlap:

parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE)











Tip



One of the useful interactive feature of parallelPlot is we can click on a variable of interest, for example Happiness score, the monotonous blue colour (default) will change a blues with different intensity colour scheme will be used.




15.5.3 Changing the colour scheme
Use the continuousCS argument to apply a different colour scale. Here, the "YlOrRd" (Yellow–Orange–Red) palette is applied:

parallelPlot(wh,
             continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
             rotateTitle = TRUE)







15.5.4 Parallel coordinates plot with histogram
Use histoVisibility to display a histogram along each variable’s axis. This helps reveal the distribution of each variable:

histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh))

parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisibility)











Note



rep(TRUE, ncol(wh)) creates a logical vector of TRUE values — one per column — enabling histograms for all variables simultaneously.

title: 6 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
Correlation coefficient is a popular statistic used to measure the type and strength of the relationship between two variables. The values of a correlation coefficient ranges between -1.0 and 1.0. A correlation coefficient of 1 shows a perfect linear relationship between the two variables, while a -1.0 shows a perfect inverse relationship between the two variables. A correlation coefficient of 0.0 shows no linear relationship between the two variables.
When multivariate data are used, the correlation coefficients of the pair comparisons are displayed in a table form known as correlation matrix or scatterplot matrix.
There are three broad reasons for computing a correlation matrix:

To reveal the relationship between high-dimensional variables pair-wisely.
To input into other analyses. For example, people commonly use correlation matrices as inputs for exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation models, and linear regression when excluding missing values pairwise.
As a diagnostic when checking other analyses. For example, with linear regression a high amount of correlations suggests that the linear regression’s estimates will be unreliable.

When the data is large, both in terms of the number of observations and the number of variables, Corrgram tend to be used to visually explore and analyse the structure and the patterns of relations among variables. It is designed based on two main schemes:

Rendering the value of a correlation to depict its sign and magnitude, and
Reordering the variables in a correlation matrix so that “similar” variables are positioned adjacently, facilitating perception.

In this hands-on exercise, you will learn how to plot data visualisation for visualising correlation matrix with R. It consists of three main sections. First, you will learn how to create correlation matrix using pairs() of R Graphics. Next, you will learn how to plot corrgram using corrplot package of R. Lastly, you will learn how to create an interactive correlation matrix using plotly R.

6.3 Importing and Preparing The Data Set
In this hands-on exercise, the Wine Quality Data Set of UCI Machine Learning Repository will be used. The data set consists of 13 variables and 6497 observations. For the purpose of this exercise, we have combined the red wine and white wine data into one data file. It is called wine_quality and is in csv file format.

6.3.1 Importing Data
First, let us import the data into R by using read_csv() of readr package.


wine <- read_csv("../Data/wine_quality.csv")


Notice that beside quality and type, the rest of the variables are numerical and continuous data type.

title: 6 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
6.4 Building Correlation Matrix: pairs() Method
There are more than one way to build scatterplot matrix with R. In this section, you will learn how to create a scatterplot matrix by using the pairs function of R Graphics.
Before you continue to the next step, you should read the syntax description of pairs function.

6.4.1 Building a Basic Correlation Matrix
The figure below shows the scatter plot matrix of Wine Quality Data. It is a 11 by 11 matrix.

pairs(wine[, 1:11])








The required input of pairs() can be a matrix or data frame. The code chunk used to create the scatterplot matrix is relatively simple. It uses the default pairs function. Columns 2 to 12 of the wine dataframe is used to build the scatterplot matrix. The variables are: fixed acidity, volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlorides, free sulfur dioxide, total sulfur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates and alcohol.

pairs(wine[, 2:12])










6.4.2 Drawing the Lower Corner
The pairs function of R Graphics provides many customisation arguments. For example, it is a common practice to show either the upper half or lower half of the correlation matrix instead of both. This is because a correlation matrix is symmetric.
To show the lower half of the correlation matrix, the upper.panel argument will be used as shown in the code chunk below.

pairs(wine[, 2:12], upper.panel = NULL)








Similarly, you can display the upper half of the correlation matrix by using the code chunk below.

pairs(wine[, 2:12], lower.panel = NULL)










6.4.3 Including Correlation Coefficients
To show the correlation coefficient of each pair of variables instead of a scatter plot, panel.cor function will be used. This will also show higher correlations in a larger font.

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep = "")
  if (missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[, 2:12],
      upper.panel = panel.cor)

title: 6 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
6.5 Visualising Correlation Matrix: ggcorrmat()
One of the major limitations of the correlation matrix is that the scatter plots appear very cluttered when the number of observations is relatively large (i.e. more than 500 observations). To overcome this problem, Corrgram data visualisation technique suggested by D. J. Murdoch and E. D. Chow (1996) and Friendly, M (2002) will be used.
There are at least three R packages that provide functions to plot corrgram, they are:

corrgram
ellipse
corrplot

On top of that, some R packages like ggstatsplot also provide functions for building corrgram.
In this section, you will learn how to visualise a correlation matrix by using ggcorrmat() of ggstatsplot package.

6.5.1 The Basic Plot
One of the advantages of using ggcorrmat() over many other methods to visualise a correlation matrix is its ability to provide a comprehensive and yet professional statistical report as shown in the figure below.

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11)









ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black",
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  title    = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are not significant at p < 0.05"
)














NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:




cor.vars argument is used to compute the correlation matrix needed to build the corrgram.
ggcorrplot.args argument provides additional (mostly aesthetic) arguments that will be passed to ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot function. The list should avoid any of the following arguments since they are already internally being used: corr, method, p.mat, sig.level, ggtheme, colors, lab, pch, legend.title, digits.



The sample sub-code chunk below can be used to control specific components of the plot such as the font size of the x-axis, y-axis, and the statistical report.

ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text = element_text(size = 5),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8)))

text:
6.6 Building Multiple Plots
Since ggstatsplot is an extension of ggplot2, it also supports faceting. However the feature is not available in ggcorrmat() but in grouped_ggcorrmat() of ggstatsplot.

grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  type = "robust",
  p.adjust.method = "holm",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2),
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black",
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  annotation.args = list(
    tag_levels = "a",
    title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
    subtitle = "The measures are: alcohol, sulphates, fixed acidity, citric acid, chlorides, residual sugar, density, free sulfur dioxide and volatile acidity",
    caption = "Dataset: UCI Machine Learning Repository"
  )
)














NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:




To build a facet plot, the only argument needed is grouping.var.
Behind grouped_ggcorrmat(), patchwork package is used to create the multiplot. plotgrid.args argument provides a list of additional arguments passed to patchwork::wrap_plots, except for the guides argument which is already separately specified earlier.
Likewise, annotation.args argument is calling plot annotation arguments of the patchwork package.

section: 6.7 Visualising Correlation Matrix using corrplot Package
text:
6.7 Visualising Correlation Matrix using corrplot Package
In this hands-on exercise, we will focus on corrplot. However, you are encouraged to explore the other two packages too.
Before getting started, you are required to read An Introduction to corrplot Package in order to gain a basic understanding of the corrplot package.

6.7.1 Getting Started with corrplot
Before we can plot a corrgram using corrplot(), we need to compute the correlation matrix of the wine data frame.
In the code chunk below, cor() of R Stats is used to compute the correlation matrix of the wine data frame.

wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11])

Next, corrplot() is used to plot the corrgram using all the default settings as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor)








Notice that the default visual object used to plot the corrgram is a circle. The default layout of the corrgram is a symmetric matrix. The default colour scheme is diverging blue-red. Blue colours are used to represent pair variables with positive correlation coefficients and red colours are used to represent pair variables with negative correlation coefficients. The intensity of the colour, also known as saturation, is used to represent the strength of the correlation coefficient. Darker colours indicate relatively stronger linear relationships between the paired variables. On the other hand, lighter colours indicate relatively weaker linear relationships.


6.7.2 Working with Visual Geometrics
In corrplot package, there are seven visual geometrics (parameter method) that can be used to encode the attribute values. They are: circle, square, ellipse, number, shade, color and pie. The default is circle. As shown in the previous section, the default visual geometric of the corrplot matrix is circle. However, this default setting can be changed by using the method argument as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "ellipse")








Feel free to change the method argument to other supported visual geometrics.


6.7.3 Working with Layout
corrplot() supports three layout types, namely: "full", "upper" or "lower". The default is "full" which displays the full matrix. The default setting can be changed by using the type argument of corrplot().

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "ellipse",
         type = "lower")








The default layout of the corrgram can be further customised. For example, arguments diag and tl.col are used to turn off the diagonal cells and to change the axis text label colour to black respectively as shown in the code chunk and figure below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "ellipse",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black")








Please feel free to experiment with other layout design arguments such as tl.pos, tl.cex, tl.offset, cl.pos, cl.cex and cl.offset, just to mention a few of them.


6.7.4 Working with Mixed Layout
With corrplot package, it is possible to design a corrgram with a mixed visual matrix on one half and a numerical matrix on the other half. In order to create a corrgram with mixed layout, corrplot.mixed(), a wrapped function for mixed visualisation style, will be used.
The figure below shows a mixed layout corrgram plotted using the wine quality data.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor,
               lower = "ellipse",
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")








Notice that arguments lower and upper are used to define the visualisation method used. In this case ellipse is used to map the lower half of the corrgram and numerical matrix (i.e. number) is used to map the upper half of the corrgram. The argument tl.pos is used to specify the placement of the axis label. Lastly, the diag argument is used to specify the glyph on the principal diagonal of the corrgram.


6.7.5 Combining Corrgram with the Significant Test
In statistical analysis, we are also interested to know which pairs of variables have statistically significant correlation coefficients.
Figure below shows a corrgram combined with the significant test. The corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statistically significant. For example, the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free sulfur dioxide is statistically significant at significant level of 0.1 but not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.









With corrplot package, we can use cor.mtest() to compute the p-values and confidence interval for each pair of variables.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level = .95)

We can then use the p.mat argument of corrplot() as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)








The corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statistically significant. For example, the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free sulfur dioxide is statistically significant at significance level of 0.1 but not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.


6.7.6 Reorder a Corrgram
Matrix reordering is very important for mining the hidden structure and pattern in a corrgram. By default, the order of attributes of a corrgram is sorted according to the correlation matrix (i.e. "original"). The default setting can be overwritten by using the order argument of corrplot(). Currently, corrplot package supports four sorting methods:

"AOE" is for the angular order of the eigenvectors. See Michael Friendly (2002) for details.
"FPC" for the first principal component order.
"hclust" for hierarchical clustering order, and "hclust.method" for the agglomeration method to be used.

"hclust.method" should be one of "ward", "single", "complete", "average", "mcquitty", "median" or "centroid".

"alphabet" for alphabetical order.

More algorithms can be found in the seriation package.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor,
               lower = "ellipse",
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order = "AOE",
               tl.col = "black")










6.7.7 Reordering a Correlation Matrix using hclust
If using hclust, corrplot() can draw rectangles around the corrgram based on the results of hierarchical clustering.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "ellipse",
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order = "hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)

11.3 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates: ggplot2 methods
A point estimate is a single number, such as a mean. Uncertainty, on the other hand, is expressed as standard error, confidence interval, or credible interval.






Important



Don’t confuse the uncertainty of a point estimate with the variation in the sample.


In this section, you will learn how to plot error bars of maths scores by race by using data provided in exam tibble data frame.
Firstly, code chunk below will be used to derive the necessary summary statistics.

my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n=n(),
    mean=mean(MATHS),
    sd=sd(MATHS)
    ) %>%
  mutate(se=sd/sqrt(n-1))

summarise() is used to compute the count of observations, mean, standard deviation,
mutate() is used to derive standard error of Maths by RACE, and
the output is saved as a tibble data table called my_sum.

11.3.1 Plotting standard error bars of point estimates
Now we are ready to plot the standard error bars of mean maths score by race as shown below.

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=RACE,
        ymin=mean-se,
        ymax=mean+se),
    width=0.2,
    colour="black",
    alpha=0.9,
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes
           (x=RACE,
            y=mean),
           stat="identity",
           color="red",
           size = 1.5,
           alpha=1) +
  ggtitle("Standard error of mean maths score by race")










NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:




The error bars are computed by using the formula mean+/-se.
For geom_point(), it is important to indicate stat=“identity”.





11.3.2 Plotting confidence interval of point estimates
Instead of plotting the standard error bar of point estimates, we can also plot the confidence intervals of mean maths score by race.

NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:

ggdist is an R package that provides a flexible set of ggplot2 geoms and stats designed especially for visualising distributions and uncertainty.
It is designed for both frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty visualization, taking the view that uncertainty visualization can be unified through the perspective of distribution visualization:
